newsitem.title: CANADA: Alberta favors chemical growth over ethane exports.
newsitem.headline: Alberta favors chemical growth over ethane exports.

text.p: Policies favoring growth in Alberta's petrochemical industry over exports of raw feedstock will continue to be the rule in the province, Alberta's new Energy Minister Steve West said.

West's long-awaited policy statement signalled a political shift for battling chemical and natural gas producing industries, which had criticized the Alberta government for creating market uncertainty by not saying which one would take precedence.
"The policies have served us well and helped foster a world class petrochemical industry which continues to grow and create jobs for Albertans. Existing policies will continue," West said.

Players in Alberta's petrochemical industry, led by NOVA Corp, are at odds with natural gas producers over whether ethane, a liquid natural gas byproduct, should be left in the province to be upgraded into ethylene and polyethylene or shipped down the proposed C$3.6 billion Alliance pipeline to Chicago.

West's predecessor, Pat Black, a strong proponent of deregulation, had wanted the industries to devise a market-driven answer among themselves rather than come out with a government-mandated solution.
West's statement left little doubt about the government's preference on the issue.
"Our goal is to maximize economic benefits from gas production and its value-added upgrading of gas liquids here in our province...," his policy statement said.

About C$1.4 billion worth of new Alberta petrochemical plants and expansions have been announced recently by NOVA, Union Carbide and Amoco Corp at a time when gas producers are itching to get better prices for their supply.

NOVA spokesman Paul Clark said a major expansion of its big ethylene complex at Joffre in central Alberta, and likely Amoco's plans to build a C$250 million plastics plant that would take in NOVA's ethylene, would have gone ahead without West's policy statement.

"One of the things the government needed clarity on was that if you were going to pull liquids out of this province, you're going to jeopardize anybody else's thinking about building here," Clark said.
Opinions differ on whether Alberta producers will be able to pump enough gas liquids in coming years for both export and future petrochemical plants.
But a tug-of-war may never happen if enough supply exists, an energy department spokewoman said.

An official with Alliance, a partnership of 18 energy companies including Alberta Energy Co Ltd, Gulf Canada Resources Ltd and IPL Energy Inc, said his group continued to believe enough liquids could be produced to supply domestic needs and export opportunities.

"The existing policies in our view accommodate both petrochemical development and our project. That we find very encouraging," Crawford said. "In fact, it's precisely what we asked the Alberta government for." ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
